 ‘Grandparent 529s Do Not Count’: Wes Moss on Why a Family With $250,000 Income Gets Zero Aid
 By Jake FitzGerald 
 Published November 21, 2026, 4:46am ET · 4 min read 
 Money Talks desk. Editor: Jake FitzGerald .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 Wes Moss says the FAFSA ignores 401(k)s, home equity and grandparent-owned 529s, so a family earning $250,000 can qualify for zero aid.
 Income and brokerage assets drive the Student Aid Index, which is why the Joneses' index of about $95,000 wipes out need while the Smiths' $4,000 leaves large need.
 The FAFSA looks back two years, so Moss's warning is that a big capital gain in that base year can add far more to aid costs than holding the investment.

 The Jones family makes $250,000, holds $1 million in a 401(k), and qualifies for zero need-based aid at a $50,000 school. The 401(k) plays no role in that result.
 Wes Moss, a certified financial planner and chief investment strategist at Capital Investment Advisors, built that example on the Nov. 17 Ask an Advisor episode of The Clark Howard Podcast . His rundown of what the FAFSA ignores was blunt: “ Grandparent-owned 529 , not counted. Home equity excluded. 401(k), IRA, Roth, not counted.” 
 The stakes come down to location. The same dollar can be invisible inside a 401(k) and costly inside a brokerage account. That difference flows straight into the Student Aid Index (SAI), the single number colleges use to set your aid.
 Moss Has the FAFSA Math Right
 Moss’s breakdown is correct for the federal form, and it is the most useful thing a family with savings can learn before filing. He said the formula weights parent income most, then parent assets, then student income, then student assets.
 Federal rules back up that order. Parent income left after allowances is taxed at rates that increase from 22% to 47% [ 1 ] , according to the federal aid handbook. Parent assets are first cut to 12% of their available value, which Moss rounds to about 3 to 6 cents on the dollar.
 His other figures are estimates: student assets count at about 20%, and roughly the first $12,000 of student income is excluded. Here is how his two families compare.

 The Smiths’ 401(k) and home equity add nothing. Their $30,000 brokerage account adds roughly $900 to $1,800 at Moss’s asset rates. That leaves a large gap the school can fill with aid.
 The Joneses face the opposite math. Their $500,000 brokerage adds roughly $15,000 to $30,000 to the SAI. The $150,000 parent-owned 529 adds another $4,500 to $9,000.
 Income does the rest. An SAI near $95,000 sits far above the sticker price, so need drops to zero.
 One gap in Moss’s list: it describes the FAFSA only. Many private colleges also require the CSS Profile, which can count home equity and other assets the federal form ignores. Check each school’s requirements before moving money.
 A Single Capital Gain Can Cost More Than the Account Itself
 Moss’s sharper warning was about timing. The FAFSA pulls income and assets from two years prior, “kind of like IRMAA,” he said. A big capital gain in that year can sharply raise what the form says you should pay.
 Consider an illustrative $50,000 gain realized in the base year. Once allowances are used up, it gets taxed as income at 22% to 47% [ 1 ] . That adds $11,000 to $23,500 to the SAI.
 Leave the same position unsold and it stays an asset. At Moss’s rates, it adds only $1,500 to $3,000. The sale year matters more than the sale itself.
 Retirees already know this trap. Medicare’s IRMAA surcharges also use income from two years back. In 2026, the first Part B surcharge starts above $109,000 single or $218,000 joint income and adds $81.20 a month on top of the $202.90 [ 2 ] standard premium.
 Moss hosts the Money Matters radio show and the Retire Sooner podcast, where he regularly works through research-driven family finance math like this.
 Five Moves to Make Before Your Base Year Locks In
 Find your first base year. A fall 2028 freshman’s FAFSA uses 2026 tax data, so any gain booked before Dec. 31 of this year lands on that form. Each later school year looks back two years the same way.
 Time big gains around that window. If you need to rebalance or trim a concentrated stock, doing it before the first base year keeps the gain off every FAFSA your child files.
 Let grandparents keep their 529 in their own name. Moss confirmed grandparent-owned accounts are excluded from the FAFSA. The simplified form also stopped treating their distributions as student income, which removed the old penalty for using them.
 Run tuition money through a 529 for the state deduction. Moss’s tip: if your state offers a deduction and the money is going to college anyway, contribute, take the deduction and pay the bill from the 529, even if it sits there only a couple of months. Confirm your state’s holding rules first.
 Price your own SAI. Enter your real numbers into the Federal Student Aid calculator at StudentAid.gov, then rerun it with a hypothetical gain added to see the cost in dollars.
 The FAFSA cares less about how much your family has saved than about which account holds it and which year you cash it out.
